title: Conversational priming payback timeline (proto)
body:
Purpose:
This note is a lightweight prototype to reason about the latency and cost tradeoffs of different conversational priming strategies and the timeline to 'pay back' priming token overhead via downstream savings (reduced re-generation, fewer turns, lower hallucination-handling, etc.). Goal is to produce a compact, shareable chart-style artifact for product/eng discussion — not a final experiment.

Key definitions / assumptions (proto):
- Priming token set: static system prompt + persona + retrieval context. Typical sizes evaluated: 200, 600, 1200 tokens.
- Token unit cost (hosted inference baseline): $0.00003 per token (example nominal). Replace with actual pricing for final.
- Average generated tokens per user-turn without priming: 120 tokens. With priming (effective), downstream generation per turn reduces by 15%–40% depending on effectiveness / use case.
- Sessions: defined as a sequence of conversational turns from start to soft timeout. We evaluate sessions-per-user-per-day scenarios: 1, 3, 10.
- Discounting: ignore time value of money; payback measured in days given an assumed conversion of daily sessions.
- Latency impact: sending prime increases request size (client -> server) but we assume server-side batching amortizes. We surface a crude delta: added token-latency cost 0.6–1.2 ms per extra 100 tokens where the runtime supports optimal kernel selection; worst-case network cost ignored here.

Methodology (sketch):
1. For each priming size (P tokens) and nominal session profile (S sessions/day, T turns/session), estimate additional cost = P * cost_per_token * S (per day).
2. Estimate downstream token savings per session based on effectiveness band: conservatively 15%, likely 25%, optimistic 40%. Savings applied to generated tokens per turn * turns per session.
3. Daily net savings = token_savings_value - priming_cost. Payback days = (priming_cost on day 1) / daily_net_savings; if daily_net_savings <= 0 then payback = infinity.
4. Produce simple ASCII tables and mini-charts to convey sensitivity.

Scenarios considered (parameters):
- Baseline per-turn gen: 120 tokens
- Turns per session: 3
- Cost per token: $0.00003
- Priming sizes: 200, 600, 1200 tokens
- Session frequency: 1/day (low), 3/day (medium), 10/day (high)
- Effectiveness bands: 15%, 25%, 40%

Representative calculations (walkthrough):
Example A: P=600 tokens, S=3 sessions/day, effectiveness=25%
- Priming cost per day = 600 tokens * $0.00003 * 3 = 600 * 0.00003 * 3 = $0.054
- Downstream generated tokens per session = 120 tokens/turn * 3 turns = 360 tokens
- Expected saved tokens per session = 360 * 0.25 = 90 tokens -> value = 90 * $0.00003 = $0.0027
- Total daily savings from reductions = $0.0027 * 3 sessions = $0.0081
- Net daily = savings - priming_cost = $0.0081 - $0.054 = -$0.0459 -> Negative: priming not paid back under these numbers

Observation: under these conservative numbers, one-time priming sent every session wastes cost. The goal is to find deployment patterns where priming is amortized (e.g., cached per-session, reused across turns, or only sent once per session rather than every request).

Amortization model variants (proto):
A) Session-only priming (send once at session start, reused for T turns) — baseline above assumes send once per session.
B) Per-request priming (send with every request) — multiply priming cost by turns per session (bad for ROI).
C) Cached KV prefetch (server holds prime cached after first call for session life) — cost = priming once per session (same as A) but reduces client bytes & network latency on mid-turn requests.
D) Adaptive priming (only send priming in first N sessions or when retrieval indicates new context) — lowers frequency S_effective of priming.

Sensitivity table (text): columns: PrimingSize | Sessions/day | Eff% | DailyPrimCost | DailySavings | NetDaily | PaybackDays
200-token priming (P=200):
- S=1, Eff=15% -> PrimCost=200*0.00003*1=$0.006 -> Savings= (360*0.15)*0.00003*1=$0.00162 -> Net=-$0.00438 -> Payback=inf
- S=3, Eff=25% -> PrimCost=200*0.00003*3=$0.018 -> Savings=(360*0.25)*0.00003*3=$0.0243 -> Net=+$0.0063 -> PaybackDays = (initial priming burden of first-day extra overhead?) For amortization we treat a 'first-day' cost of priming*1 session vs ongoing savings; approximate payback = PrimCost / NetDaily = 0.018 / 0.0063 ≈ 2.9 days
600-token priming (P=600):
- S=3, Eff=25% -> PrimCost=$0.054 -> Savings=$0.0081 -> Net=-$0.0459 -> Payback=inf
600-token priming, S=10, Eff=40% -> PrimCost=600*0.00003*10=$0.18 -> Savings=(360*0.4)*0.00003*10 = (144*0.00003*10) = $0.0432 -> Net=-$0.1368 -> Payback=inf (still negative)
1200-token priming (P=1200):
- S=10, Eff=40% -> PrimCost=1200*0.00003*10=$0.36 -> Savings=(360*0.4)*0.00003*10=$0.0432 -> Net=-$0.3168 -> Payback=inf

Takeaway: with these token-price assumptions, naive large priming per session is hard to justify unless one of the following is true:
- Priming is reused across many sessions (global caching) so the cost amortizes over many days/users.
- Effectiveness produces much larger downstream token reductions (e.g., >80% in narrow Q&A or retrieval-augmented completion).
- Priming prevents third-party API calls, reduces human-in-loop escalations, or reduces expensive multimodal generation steps (non-token dollar savings).

Quick ASCII payoff sketch (net daily $ for P=200,600,1200 across S=1,3,10 and Eff=25%):
Net daily $ (rows=S, cols=P):
S=1: | P=200: -0.0044 | P=600: -0.0132 | P=1200: -0.0264
S=3: | P=200: +0.0063 | P=600: -0.0459 | P=1200: -0.0918
S=10:| P=200: +0.033 | P=600: -0.0459 | P=1200: -0.163

Mini-interpretation: small priming (200 tokens) can pay back in medium-frequency sessions with moderate effectiveness; larger priming must be justified by reuse or by improving downstream turn-level compression dramatically.

Latency notes (qualitative):
- Client to server payload adds priming tokens. If we send priming once per session, the initial-turn latency increases proportionally to token-serialization + network time. In many UIs that's acceptable if subsequent turns are fast.
- If per-request priming is used, user-perceived latency grows and combining priming with streaming and partial decode can be required.
- Server-side caching/pinning makes the best UX tradeoff: one heavier first call, then lightweight incremental requests.

Recommendations for next steps (experiments to run):
1) Recompute with actual token pricing from hosted product billing and our Dedicated/Private unit economics (per-GPU amortized cost). This doc assumes only per-token variable cost; infra-fixed cost could change thresholds.
2) Run A/B on a narrowly scoped flow (helpdesk-FAQ retrieval) where retrieval quality combined with a 600-token prime is expected to yield high reduction in downstream length (empirical effect might be 60–80%). Measure real token-savings and reduction in support escalations.
3) Evaluate caching strategies: per-session cache TTL, per-user cross-session cache, and retrieval-triggered re-prime. Track cache hit-rate and bandwidth cost.
4) Latency bench: measure first-turn delta vs subsequent-turn delta in both hosted and Dedicated; include network serialization overhead for big primes.
5) Instrument long-tail: examine cohort of sessions where priming caused a reduction in follow-up clarifying turns (this captures value beyond raw tokens).

Notes to reviewers / open questions:
- We used a constant tokens-per-turn; conversational length distributions are heavy-tailed — need percentile-based analysis.
- Cost-per-token is significantly different across model sizes and quantization; for Dedicated pricing the marginal token-dollar may be lower. Should fold in model-size sensitivity (e.g., chat-7B vs chat-70B).
- There are non-token savings (human escalation, external API calls) which can dominate. Consider hybrid currency: token-$ + ops-$ in final model.

Appendix: small ascii timeline example (P=200, S=3, Eff=25%)
Day 0: one-time priming cost = $0.018 (three sessions day 0 assumed)
Day by day net cumulative:
Day 1: net += +$0.0063 -> cum = -$0.0117
Day 2: net += +$0.0063 -> cum = -$0.0054
Day 3: net += +$0.0063 -> cum = +$0.0009 -> payback reached around day 3

Visual bar (simple):
Payback window (days) for P=200,S=3,25%: [ - - | - | + ] -> ~3 days

Draft action items:
- (Marco) run a quick price-recalc with Dedicated token marginal costs and update table (due 2029-08-08).
- (Aisha) prototype a small A/B on helpdesk retrieval flow with P=200 and P=600 primes, record token counts and escalation rate (due 2029-08-20).
- (Diego) add latency microbench for first-turn vs cached-turn across regions and include p95/p99 (due 2029-08-12).

If reviewers prefer, I can convert the sensitivity tables into CSV-style text for ingestion into quick notebooks. This doc intentionally keeps numbers crude to force design-level decisions rather than exact thresholds.

End of proto.
